title: Passing the Treaty
narration_text: Congratulations! You've passed a one percent treaty. Now you've got twenty-seven point two billion dollars per year flowing into the one percent Treaty Fund.
context: The narrator announces the successful passage of the one percent treaty and the resulting annual funding.

title: Human Involvement
narration_text: That's the good news. The bad news is that humans are involved.
context: The narrator notes that the involvement of humans complicates the allocation of the treaty funds.

title: Automatic Deductions
narration_text: Not all of it is available for allocation. First, the automatic deductions (think of these as the "cost of convincing humans to stop killing each other" tax):
context: Introduction to the various mandatory deductions that reduce the total fund before allocation.

title: Victory Bond Repayment
narration_text: VICTORY Incentive Alignment Bond investors receive ten percent, or two point seven two billion dollars, to repay campaign funders.
context: Describing the first deduction meant to repay the investors who funded the campaign.

title: Political Alignment
narration_text: Political incentives from Incentive Alignment Bonds receive ten percent, or two point seven two billion dollars, to keep politicians aligned.
context: Detailing the second deduction used to ensure politicians remain aligned with the treaty's goals.

title: Wishocracy's Share
narration_text: Eighty percent, or twenty-one point eight billion dollars, is available for Wishocracy as the amount you get to allocate.
context: Revealing the final amount available for allocation through the Wishocracy system.

title: Resisting Special Interests
narration_text: How do you stop parasitic special interests from stealing that twenty-one point eight billion dollars? If history is any guide, you don't.
context: The narrator questions how to protect the fund from lobbyists and special interest groups.

title: Lobbyist Ants
narration_text: Every pool of money humanity has ever created has attracted lobbyists the way a dropped ice cream cone attracts ants, except ants at least work hard.
context: A cynical comparison between the behavior of lobbyists and ants attracted to sugar.

title: Code vs Committees
narration_text: Wishocracy replaces committees with code and representatives with mathematics. It lets eight billion people collectively decide how to spend
context: Explaining how Wishocracy uses mathematics and code to bypass traditional bureaucratic hurdles.

title: Avoiding Nightmares
narration_text: twenty-one point eight billion dollars without turning it into a bureaucratic nightmare.
context: Emphasizing that the system allows for mass decision-making without creating inefficiency.

title: The Stomach Analogy
narration_text: The difference between this and the N.I.H. is like asking two hundred bureaucrats what you should have for lunch versus asking your stomach.
context: A humorous comparison between centralized government research funding and biological instinct.

title: Professional Courtesy
narration_text: Your stomach has never once funded a colleague's lunch out of professional courtesy.
context: The narrator highlights the lack of political bias in biological needs compared to bureaucracies.

title: Branding Wishonia
narration_text: On my home planet (also called Wishonia, because we named the system after ourselves, which your species would call "branding"),
context: The narrator shares background information about their home planet's naming and culture.

title: Alien Wishocracy
narration_text: we've been running Wishocracy for four thousand two hundred and ninety-seven years. It still works.
context: Providing historical proof of Wishocracy's longevity and success on the narrator's home world.

title: Allocation Method
narration_text: How Wishocracy Allocates the one percent Treaty Fund: Decentralized Crowdfunding.
context: Introducing the specific mechanism of decentralized crowdfunding used to allocate funds.

title: Campaign Proposals
narration_text: Your decentralized institutes of health network functions as a decentralized crowdfunding platform. Anyone can submit a campaign proposal.
context: Explaining the open-access nature of the platform where anyone can propose a project.

title: Competing Campaigns
narration_text: Wishocracy allocates funds from the one percent Treaty Fund across competing campaigns.
context: Detailing how the funds are spread across various health-related proposals.

title: Global Kickstarter
narration_text: It's Kickstarter, but backed by the G.D.P. of nations instead of your friend's credit card.
context: A modern comparison to help humans understand the scale and security of the funding.

title: Automated FDA
narration_text: What your decentralized F.D.A. handles automatically (no voting required):
context: Defining the processes that are handled algorithmically without the need for collective voting.

title: Testing Choices
narration_text: For which treatments get tested, companies register and patients choose (capitalism doing something useful).
context: Explaining how market forces and patient choice determine which treatments enter testing.

title: Diseases and Mortality
narration_text: For which diseases get researched, patients join trials for their conditions (people tend to be motivated about their own mortality).
context: Describing how patient participation drives the direction of disease research.

title: Resource Allocation
narration_text: Resource allocation within trials is handled by market prices and participant choices.
context: Detailing how resources within medical trials are distributed through market mechanics.

title: Wishocracy's Hard Decisions
narration_text:
What Wishocracy Actually Decides:

The hard stuff. Allocation across campaign proposals competing for one percent Treaty Fund funds:
context: Defining the core subjective decisions that the Wishocracy system handles.

title: Infrastructure Plumbing
narration_text:
Infrastructure Campaigns (the boring but essential plumbing).

The Decentralized Framework for Drug Assessment Development has a one billion dollar per year proposal.
context: Listing the necessary infrastructure projects that require large-scale funding.

title: EHR Integration
narration_text: The Epic electronic health records, or E.H.R. integration project, is five million dollars one-time.
context: A specific one-time funding proposal for health record system integration.

title: AWS Services
narration_text: Amazon Web Services, or A.W.S. infrastructure services, is three million dollars per year.
context: Mentioning the recurring cost for cloud infrastructure to support the system.

title: Security Audit
narration_text: The Security Audit Program is two million dollars per year.
context: Detailing the annual cost for maintaining the security of the decentralized health network.

title: FDA Competition
narration_text: An alternative decentralized F.D.A. is eight million dollars per year (competition! novel concept for government!).
context: The narrator mocks the government's lack of competition while introducing a funded alternative.

title: Public Goods
narration_text: Public Goods (things the market won't fund because nobody gets rich curing diseases that don't sell pills).
context: Defining the 'Public Goods' category, which covers non-profitable medical research.

title: Trial Subsidies
narration_text: "Patient Trial Subsidies Program" — eight hundred million dollars per year (automatic formula).
context: A fund set aside to help patients participate in clinical trials.

title: Off-Patent Research
narration_text: "Off-Patent Drug Research" — twenty billion dollars per year.
context: A massive allocation for researching drugs that are no longer protected by patents.

title: Rare Diseases and Failures
narration_text:
"Rare Disease Initiative" — ten billion dollars per year.

"Negative Results Publishing Fund" — five billion dollars per year
context: Allocations for rare diseases and the crucial sharing of failed experimental data.

title: Value of Negative Results
narration_text: (yes, knowing what *doesn't* work is worth billions; your species keeps re-running failed experiments because nobody publishes failures).
context: The narrator criticizes humanity's habit of repeating mistakes due to hidden negative data.

title: Service Bidding
narration_text:
Service Provider Bids (capitalism, but supervised).

"Data Storage Provider A" — two billion dollars per year.
context: Explaining the supervised bidding process for service providers within the system.

title: Storage Competition
narration_text: "Data Storage Provider B" — one point five billion dollars per year (competing).
context: Showing how competition between providers keeps the costs of the infrastructure down.

title: Pragmatic Insurance Pool
narration_text:
"Pragmatic Clinical Trial Insurance Pool" — ten billion dollar reserve.

How It Works: Pairwise Comparisons Between Campaigns.
context: Introducing the 10 billion dollar Pragmatic Clinical Trial Insurance Pool and its fundamental operational mechanism.

title: Committees Fail
narration_text: No committee on Earth has ever looked at a list of ten thousand proposals and made a good decision. Committees are where good ideas go to die of old age.
context: Explaining why traditional committees fail at making good decisions when faced with large numbers of proposals.

title: Pairwise Comparisons
narration_text:
Instead, the global population votes using pairwise comparisons:

"What's more important right now:"
context: Introducing the concept of pairwise comparisons as an alternative to committee-based decision making.

title: Priority Trade-offs
narration_text:
"Framework for drug assessment development" versus "Alzheimer's prize"?

"Epic integration" versus "Security audits"?
context: Giving specific examples of the trade-offs voters might face between infrastructure and medical prizes.

title: Research Allocations
narration_text:
"Rare disease research" versus "An alternative drug assessment framework"?

"Patient subsidies" versus "Infrastructure spending"?
context: Further examples of pairwise choices between research goals and infrastructure spending.

title: Preferred Funding
narration_text: Millions of people make simple pairwise choices. The algorithm aggregates preferences into funding allocations. No filibustering.
context: Describing how mass participation in simple choices leads to definitive funding allocations without political delays.

title: No More Filibustering
narration_text:
No horse-trading. No senators holding medical research hostage because they want a highway in their district.

Why You Can't Just Use a Spreadsheet.
context: Emphasizing that this method removes political obstacles like filibustering and district-based pork-barrel politics.

title: Implementation Choices
narration_text:
Someone is going to ask, "Why not just write a formula?" Because the decisions look like this:

One. Multiple competing implementations —
context: Addressing the question of why a simple formula isn't sufficient for complex implementation choices.

title: Team Competition
narration_text: Three teams want to build the drug assessment platform. Which one? All three? Two? The one with the best logo?
context: Illustrating the difficulty of choosing between different teams proposing the same infrastructure projects.

title: Valuation Trade-offs
narration_text: Two. Trade-offs between prizes — one hundred billion dollars for aging reversal or fifty billion dollars for Alzheimer's plus fifty billion dollars for cancer?
context: Humanity must decide how to value general versus specific medical research outcomes.

title: Collective Values
narration_text: There is no "correct" answer. There is only what humanity collectively values, which is exactly what Wishocracy measures.
context: Explaining that the goal is not a formulaic 'correct' answer, but a measurement of collective human values.

title: Public Goods
narration_text: Three. Public goods allocation — How much for off-patent drugs versus rare diseases? Markets won't answer this because there's no profit in it.
context: Highlighting where markets fail, such as in the funding of off-patent drugs and rare disease research.

title: Service Competition
narration_text: Four. Service provider competition — Which companies get contracts for what amounts?
context: Managing the competitive bidding process between different service providers within the system.

title: Steering and Engines
narration_text: Your decentralized F.D.A. allocates resources WITHIN pragmatic clinical trials. Wishocracy allocates resources BETWEEN campaigns.
context: Defining the separate roles of the decentralized FDA and Wishocracy in resource allocation.

title: Steering the Wheel
narration_text: One is the engine, the other is the steering wheel. You need both unless you enjoy driving into walls.
context: An analogy explaining why both clinical trial management and overarching priority setting are necessary.

title: Simple Voting
narration_text: The core of Wishocracy is a voting method so simple, even a congressman could do it (though we'd recommend they practice first).
context: Humorously describing the core simplicity of the Wishocracy voting system.

title: APPA
narration_text: It's called Aggregated Pairwise Preference Allocation, or simply, the Pairwise Slider Allocation.
context: Formally naming the voting method used by the Wishocracy platform.

title: Comparison Strength
narration_text: Your brain can't rank a list of twenty priorities. It gives up around item number seven. But it's fantastic at comparing two things.
context: Cognitive science justification for using pairwise comparisons over traditional list-based ranking.

title: The System Question
narration_text:
Instead of asking, "Rank these ten thousand campaign proposals," the system asks:

"What's more important right now:
context: Showing how the system reduces massive complexity into a single, simple question for the voter.

title: Making the Choice
narration_text:
decentralized F.D.A. protocol development or security audits?"

You make a choice. That's it. You do this a few times with different random pairs.
context: Describing the user experience of making quick choices between randomly presented infrastructure pairs.

title: Speed of Input
narration_text: It takes five minutes. Less time than you spend choosing a Netflix show, and considerably more important. Millions of other people do the same.
context: Putting the voter's time commitment into perspective compared to trivial daily choices.

title: Real-time Ranking
narration_text: An algorithm takes all these simple, head-to-head comparisons and builds a real-time ranking of infrastructure and public goods priorities.
context: Explaining how the algorithm transforms individual votes into a global priority list.

title: Infrastructure Focus
narration_text: (Remember: Wishocracy doesn't allocate between diseases. Patients do that by choosing which trials to join.
context: Clarifying that Wishocracy does not pick winning diseases; it sets up the infrastructure for research.

title: Market Limits
narration_text: Wishocracy allocates between *infrastructure campaigns* and *public goods* that markets can't handle.).
context: Defining the specific target of Wishocracy's allocation: non-marketable public goods.

title: Crowds and Math
narration_text:
It's the wisdom of crowds, but without the crowds having to talk to each other.

Why This Actually Works (Math Warning).
context: Transitioning to the mathematical and statistical reasons why the Wisdom of Crowds is effective in this context.

title: Preventing Gaming
narration_text:
Random pairs prevent gaming.
You can't lobby five million people.
Well, you can try.
Good luck.
context: Explaining how the randomness of the pairing prevents special interest groups from manipulating the results.

title: Preference Extraction
narration_text: Statistical models (Bradley-Terry, PageRank) extract global preferences from individual comparisons.
context: Mentioning the specific mathematical models used to synthesize individual choices into global priorities.

title: Google for Health
narration_text:
The same math that ranks Google search results can rank humanity's medical priorities.
Google uses it to find cat videos.
context: Drawing a comparison between the ranking of internet search results and human medical priorities.

title: Canceling Outliers
narration_text:
You'll use it to cure cancer.
Progress.

Outliers cancel out.
The guy who votes "fund my personal jetpack" gets drowned out
context: Describing how mass participation filters out nonsensical or purely selfish outlier requests.

title: Reliable Wisdom
narration_text:
by the millions voting for "cure my mother's Alzheimer's.".

Wisdom of crowds emerges.
Reliably.
context: The emergence of collective focus on shared human needs over individual eccentricities.

title: The Math Example
narration_text:
Repeatedly.
Boringly.

Example with real numbers:

five million people vote.
Each makes twenty comparisons.
context: Providing a numerical scale of how much data the system collects from its participants.

title: Rapid Processing
narration_text:
That's one hundred million data points.

Algorithm processes them in seconds.
context: Concluding with the efficiency of modern computation in processing vast amounts of human preference data.

title: Budget Output Starts
narration_text: Output: "Allocate forty percent to patient subsidy programs, twenty-five percent to decentralized F.D.A. protocol development,
context: The system begins outputting the budget results calculated from millions of individual crowd-sourced inputs.

title: Continuing the Budget
narration_text: fifteen percent to off-patent drug research, ten percent to rare disease initiatives, five percent to security infrastructure,
context: The AI continues reading out the specific percentage allocations for the healthcare budget.

title: Budget Finalized
narration_text:
five percent to negative results publishing...".

No committee meetings were harmed in the making of this budget.
context: The final budget items are listed followed by a humorous remark about the lack of bureaucratic interference.

title: Distributed Stupidity
narration_text: It's democracy without the shouting. The stupidity is still there, but it's evenly distributed across millions of people and thus cancels out.
context: The narrator explains the theory behind the system: mass participation offsets individual human errors.

title: The Wisdom of Crowds
narration_text: This is called "the wisdom of crowds." It works for the same reason that guessing the weight of a cow at a fair works:
context: Introducing a classic statistical analogy to explain why the Wishocracy system is accurate.

title: Collective Accuracy
narration_text: individually you're all terrible at it, but collectively you're weirdly accurate. About half of the ten thousand civilizations
context: Describing the paradox of group accuracy versus individual failure in estimation tasks.

title: Interstellar Voting Habits
narration_text:
I've worked with use some version of this.
The other half voted against it, which turned out to be the last thing they voted on.
context: The narrator adds a dark joke about alien civilizations that failed to adopt collective decision-making.

title: Priorities to Projects
narration_text:
From Priorities to Projects (Where Wishes Become Tasks).

Great, so the Pairwise Slider Allocation tells you "Curing Alzheimer's"
context: Transitioning from the abstract voting phase to the practical implementation phase of the system.

title: Wish vs Plan
narration_text: is a top priority. Wonderful. Now what? Having a priority without a plan is just a wish. And wishes, as a rule, don't cure anything.
context: Critiquing the difference between simply wanting something and having a concrete plan to achieve it.

title: Wishocracy in Action
narration_text:
Wishocracy translates that priority into action.

A.I. Breaks It Down: An A.I. takes the impossible goal of "Cure Alzheimer's"
context: Explaining how the AI begins the decomposition of a massive medical goal into manageable parts.

title: Deconstructing Alzheimer's
narration_text:
and breaks it into thousands of smaller, concrete, fundable tasks.

"Cure Alzheimer's" becomes "Map protein structures."
context: Showing how a vague goal is turned into a specific scientific requirement.

title: Possible Steps
narration_text: That becomes "Run AlphaFold on these sequences." That becomes "Rent computing time." Every impossible problem is just a series
context: Continuing the breakdown into granular technical tasks that can be easily funded and executed.

title: Pyramid Wisdom
narration_text:
of possible steps arranged in a line.

Your species figured this out for building pyramids four thousand five hundred years ago
context: Comparing modern project management to the organizational feats of the ancient Egyptians.

title: The Bounty Board
narration_text:
but keeps forgetting to apply it to medicine.

The Bounty Board: The system posts these tasks to a global marketplace.
context: Introducing the global marketplace where decomposed tasks are offered to the public.

title: Saving Humanity Marketplace
narration_text:
It's eBay, but for saving humanity.

WANTED: A cure for Alzheimer's. BOUNTY: ten billion dollars.

WANTED: A map of all protein
context: Providing examples of the massive financial rewards offered for solving specific medical milestones.

title: The World Competes
narration_text:
misfolding patterns. BOUNTY: five hundred million dollars.

The World Competes: The best teams from around the world,
context: Highlighting how the bounty system attracts talent from everywhere on the planet.

title: Global Bidding
narration_text: from M.I.T. to some kid in a garage in Lagos, bid on these tasks. The system funds multiple approaches in parallel.
context: Describing the diverse range of participants and the parallel funding model.

title: Venture Capital for Health
narration_text:
The ones that show promise get more funding. The ones that fail lose funding instantly.

It's venture capital, but for not dying.
context: Explaining the ruthless but efficient Darwinian funding system applied to medical research.

title: Applying Consumer Logic
narration_text: Your species already uses this method to decide which restaurants survive and which phone apps get downloaded. Time to try it with the thing that kills you.
context: The narrator concludes that humans should use the same market logic for medicine that they use for trivial apps.
